paras: The bloodhound pursuit of Tom Brounell and Bob Riching took place on the night of February 20, 1881, when a mounted party with five bloodhounds chased the two Black men down the Brunson turnpike near Brunson's, South Carolina. The dogs threw the men to the ground after a three-mile chase, and they were arrested and jailed on a charge of store robbery. Papers in Illinois and Virginia reprinted the story as an "exciting chase," and at least one comment column mocked it as a revival of slave hunting.

According to a dispatch dated Brunson's, February 21, Brounell and Riching were accused of breaking into a store near the town on Saturday night and carrying off about one hundred dollars' worth of goods. The dispatch said the two were "at once suspicioned of the robbery" and gave no other evidence against them.

On the following night it was "understood" that the men were making their way down the Brunson turnpike toward Columbia, and a party was "quickly organized and mounted" with five trained bloodhounds. After about three miles the dogs sighted the men, who tried to outrun them; as they climbed a slight hill, two of the hounds "pounced upon the fugitives" and threw them to the ground. The hunters then came up, arrested the two men and had them "promptly put in jail," and several people along the road joined the chase.
No report of an indictment or trial for Brounell and Riching appears in the coverage, and the dispatch does not say whether either man was hurt.

The Chicago Daily Tribune printed the dispatch first, on February 23, under the headline "With Bloodhounds. Exciting Chase After Two Negro Burglar." Its prose treated the hunt as sport: the hounds followed the scent "with savage delight," the men were called "darkies" and the dogs' "prey," and the two were praised as "the best pedestrians in the country." The Alexandria Gazette reran it on February 28 as "Hunted with Bloodhounds," placing it "last week," and the Canton Register in Illinois printed it unheadlined among filler items on March 4.

The only dissenting note was sarcasm in a "Current Comment" column credited to the Philadelphia Evening News and run by the Smyrna Times in Delaware on March 9. It said Brunson people were "reviving the chivalrous sport of hunting negroes with bloodhounds," with fleeing thieves taking the place of fugitive slaves. No account of the chase from a South Carolina paper appears in the coverage.

bases: A mounted party with five bloodhounds tracked and ran down two Black men suspected of a store burglary, the dogs threw them to the ground and the hunters arrested and jailed them; no killing, threat to kill or reported injury (A1).
All copies (A1, A2, A3) reproduce one Brunson's dispatch, and the only other item (A4) is a comment on that story, so there is no independent report.

accounts.label: Brunson's dispatch (pursuers' version)
accounts.gist: Two Black men who robbed a store fled down the turnpike; a mounted party with five bloodhounds ran them down after three miles, the dogs threw them to the ground, and they were arrested and jailed.

accounts.gist: Brunson people were reviving the 'chivalrous sport' of hunting Black people with bloodhounds, with fleeing thieves in place of fugitive slaves.

framing.detail: Headlined 'With Bloodhounds. Exciting Chase After Two Negro Burglar.', the dispatch narrates the hunt as sport, with hounds following the scent 'with savage delight' and the men called 'darkies' and 'prey'.
The dispatch was rerun as 'Hunted with Bloodhounds' in Alexandria and without a headline among filler items in an Illinois weekly.
A one-line sarcastic comment called it 'reviving the chivalrous sport of hunting negroes with bloodhounds', comparing it to slave-catching.

conflicts.note: Wording variation among copies of one dispatch; the earliest copy (A1) says 'near here', consistent with a chase along the turnpike out of town.
